item.title: The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents
item.dc:creator: Uri Oren
item.description:
Lab research shows how device code phishing, a technique that applies to any device-flow client, can extend to AI coding agents, using GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example.

The post The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent
  2. How the attack works
  3. One approval, four ways the impact can spread
  4. Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal
  5. Mitigation and protection guidance
  6. References
  7. Learn More

Device code phishing has become a recurring route to account takeover. Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Notable earlier campaigns such as EvilTokens show how readily this technique can be scaled to do real damage. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026.

That led us to a different question: what else can an attacker do with a phished device code authorization? What happens when the same trick targets an AI agent rather than a mailbox?

We used GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. Depending on its configuration, it can work with code, run commands on a user’s machine, retain context across sessions, and allow an active session to be steered remotely. Like many command-line tools, it supports the OAuth device flow for sign-in. The phishing technique itself is not specific to GitHub or Copilot CLI: any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way, and the attacker chooses the requested scopes when starting the flow.

We explored this scenario in a controlled lab simulation. A victim test account approved a GitHub device-code request initiated by an attacker client we controlled. With that approval, we were able to analyze four possible outcomes:

  • Steer an active Copilot CLI session remotely, if the user has enabled remote control and organization policy allows it, and, subject to local permissions and approval settings, have the agent run commands on the user’s machine.
  • Add misleading entries to the agent’s memory that could influence later interactions.
  • Read Copilot CLI sessions that were synchronized to the cloud.
  • Access private repositories available to the affected account.

These are proof-of-concept results showing how existing features, working as designed, could be abused after a phished authorization; they are not attacks we have observed in the wild. These outcomes require the victim user to approve a device code request initiated by the attacker; each outcome also depends on the account permissions and enabled features described below.

Later in this post, we show how Microsoft Defender helps detect these attacks by connecting phishing attempts with GitHub authentication activity, and how organizations can disrupt suspicious access to protect affected identities.

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

The OAuth device flow helps clients such as command-line tools sign in without displaying a full browser. A client requests a short code; the user enters it on the service’s verification page; the requesting client receives access after approval. In device code phishing, the attacker starts the request and persuades someone else to approve it.

Microsoft has reported device code phishing against accounts in several campaigns, including Storm-2372, an AI-enabled campaign in 2026, and EvilTokens. Those cases motivated us to examine a different target: a coding agent that can work with repositories and, when remote control is enabled, expose an active session to remote interaction.

The remainder of this post describes a controlled GitHub Copilot CLI simulation; we have not observed the four outcomes below in those campaigns or in the wild.

How the attack works

  1. Initiate: The attacker starts a device-code sign-in request. In our simulation, we used the Copilot CLI client, but any device-flow client could be used.
  2. Lure: The attacker sends the short code and GitHub verification link to the user, for example under the pretext of an IT request or a Copilot license check. The verification page is genuinely hosted by GitHub; the legitimate domain alone does not establish who initiated the request.
  3. Approve: The user opens the GitHub page, signs in if needed, and approves the request. This is the social engineering step.
  1. Sign in: After approval, the attacker-controlled client completes the sign-in automatically.
  2. Operate: The attacker can act within the permissions granted to the application and the resources available to the affected account.

The request behind the code

The following example shows the initial HTTP request to GitHub’s device authorization endpoint. The Copilot CLI client identifier is public; it is not a client secret. The attacker sends the short code returned by GitHub to the user. Once the user approves it, the requesting client signs in without another manual step.

GitHub Device Code Authentication (Simplified)
Endpoint: GitHub Device Authorization Endpoint
Client ID: 
Requested scopes:

The request looks legitimate

The user signs in on the real GitHub site, not a lookalike page. A familiar domain therefore cannot tell the user whether the request was theirs. An authorization also appears under a legitimate application name; the name alone cannot distinguish the attacker-controlled client from an expected sign-in.

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

The device code approval was only the starting point. What an attacker could do next depended on the account’s permissions, enabled features, memory settings, and whether an active session could be controlled remotely.

1. An attacker can steer an enabled remote session

Copilot CLI supports remote steering of an active interactive session when the user has enabled remote control for that session and organization policy allows it. In our lab, the attacker-controlled client used the test account’s authorization to interact with a remotely controllable session. The agent ran a command on the test machine, subject to the session’s approval prompts and local operating-system permissions. This demonstrates misuse of an authorized remote-session capability working as designed; it is not unauthenticated remote code execution and does not apply when remote control is disabled, the session is not running, or the machine is offline.

2. Memory can carry the attack forward

Copilot Memory can retain repository facts and user preferences. In the simulation, we added misleading entries using the agent’s /memory command. If those entries are used in later interactions, the effects can outlast the initial sign-in. The behavior depends on which memory features and policies are enabled.

3. Synced sessions reveal earlier context

Where cloud session storage is enabled, we could read the test account’s synced Copilot CLI sessions, including sessions from before the simulation. They may contain code snippets, file paths, architecture discussions, and other work context. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, availability depends on the organization’s session-storage policy; syncing a session does not itself enable remote control.

4. Repository access follows the account

In the lab, the authorization let us access private repositories available to the test account. The request included the repo scope along with read:user, read:org, gist, and codespace. These scopes are chosen by the client that starts the flow; the resulting repository access reflects the requested scopes and the account’s permissions, not a property of Copilot CLI itself. The potential exposure is bounded by the account’s repository access, which can include application code and infrastructure definitions.

A phishing message, a click, and a GitHub authorization can each look unremarkable on their own. The challenge for defenders is recognizing when they belong to the same attempted takeover. The legitimate verification page is part of the story, not evidence that the request was safe.

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Microsoft Defender helps organizations detect and respond to device code phishing targeting GitHub accounts. With the GitHub Enterprise Cloud connector enabled in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, organizations gain visibility into GitHub activity that can support investigations of suspicious authorization patterns.

As part of our research, we developed two detections for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing, covering attacks delivered through email and Microsoft Teams.

These detections correlate suspicious messages and clicks with subsequent GitHub OAuth token creation and regeneration events, helping identify potentially unauthorized Copilot CLI authorizations that might otherwise appear legitimate. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below.

Beyond detection, we also developed a disruption action for GitHub Enterprise Managed Users (EMU). This action suspends the affected managed identity through the organization’s identity provider, interrupting the attacker’s access. We validated this capability in our research environment.

Responders should also review and revoke unexpected OAuth authorizations, verify that access is blocked, and investigate potentially affected sessions, repositories, and saved memory.

Together, these capabilities help security teams move from identifying a potential phishing attempt to containing the affected identity. Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites.

Mitigation and protection guidance

  • Make the approval rule clear to everyone who uses developer and AI tools: enter a device code only for a sign-in you initiated yourself. An unexpected request to “verify” GitHub or activate Copilot should be treated as a phishing attempt, even if the page is hosted on github.com. GitHub’s own verification page warns users never to use a code sent by someone else.
  • Configure Safe Links policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 for email and verify Safe Links protection for Microsoft Teams. These protections can help with malicious links and provide investigation context; a legitimate GitHub verification URL still requires the user to recognize an unsolicited code request.
  • Review GitHub Copilot CLI session settings. For organization-provided seats, GitHub’s “Store local sessions in the Cloud” policy determines whether sessions can be stored and remotely controlled. Choose the least permissive setting that supports your workflows. Remote control also requires an active, online interactive session.
  • Review authorized OAuth applications in GitHub account settings and revoke authorizations that are unexpected or no longer needed. Limit repository access with appropriate organization roles so an affected account cannot reach more code than its work requires.
  • If Copilot Memory is enabled, use GitHub’s memory-management controls to review and remove suspicious repository facts or user preferences. Disabling memory does not automatically delete entries already stored, so review the saved content during incident response.
  • Connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps and validate the activity available in your environment before relying on it for investigations.

Remember: A legitimate sign-in can still be the wrong one

The most striking part of this simulation was how little needed to look suspicious. The user visited the real GitHub site and approved a normal-looking request. Yet the approval belonged to a client the user had not started. From there, the consequences depended on what that identity could access and which Copilot CLI capabilities were enabled.

That is why this is more than a story about a code. As AI agents gain access to repositories, session history, and local tools, the impact of a phished authorization increasingly depends on what those agents can reach.

A legitimate verification page does not mean the request is safe. Users should approve only device-code requests they initiated. Organizations should regularly review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorizations, restrict Copilot session and memory settings to what their workflows require, and validate GitHub activity visibility in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to support investigations.

Ultimately, protecting against device code phishing requires both user awareness and the ability to connect suspicious authorization activity to the phishing attempt that preceded it.

MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed

These mappings describe behaviors demonstrated in the proof-of-concept simulation, not an attributed campaign.

  • T1566.002 – Phishing: Spearphishing Link (Initial Access). In the tested email delivery, a link led the user to the device authorization page and prompted approval.
  • T1528 – Steal Application Access Token (Credential Access). After the test account approved the request, the attacker-controlled client obtained an OAuth token.

References

  1. Authorizing OAuth apps. GitHub Docs. Explains the OAuth device authorization flow, including how users approve requests and how applications obtain access tokens.
  2. Authenticating GitHub Copilot CLI. GitHub Docs. Describes the supported authentication methods for GitHub Copilot CLI.
  3. Remote control of GitHub Copilot CLI sessions. GitHub Docs. Explains how active Copilot CLI sessions can be accessed and controlled remotely, including relevant prerequisites.
  4. GitHub Copilot session data. GitHub Docs. Provides information about session history and cloud synchronization in GitHub Copilot CLI.
  5. Managing Copilot Memory for an enterprise, organization, or repository. GitHub Docs. Describes how administrators can manage memory settings and stored information.
  6. Reviewing your authorized OAuth apps. GitHub Docs. Explains how users can review and revoke OAuth application authorizations.
  7. Repository roles for an organization. GitHub Docs. Describes repository permission levels and how organizations can limit access according to user responsibilities.
  8. Protect your GitHub Enterprise environment. Microsoft Learn. Explains how to connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to gain visibility into GitHub activity and support security investigations.
  9. Configure Safe Links policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Microsoft Learn. Provides configuration guidance for Safe Links protection against malicious URLs.

Learn More

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

item.title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors
item.dc:creator: Microsoft Security Research
item.description:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a high-volume phishing campaign using Microsoft 365 outage-themed lures to target organizations across multiple sectors worldwide.

The post High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. Phishing attack overview
  2. Attack chain overview
  3. Mitigation and protection guidance
  4. References
  5. Learn More

On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The threat actors used phishing emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to lure recipients into clicking a malicious link. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures.

Microsoft identified the threat actor’s use of specific sender domain names, randomized outage subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to make the messages appear relevant while complicating simple pattern matching. We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext.

If credentials were entered, organizations should consider the risk of account compromise, mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation, and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. We will continue to monitor this campaign and other related threats. Security teams can use Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR capabilities to investigate messages, URLs, clicks, and potential follow-on activity.

Phishing attack overview

Microsoft analyzed the email lures sent on November 13, 2026: the emails used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Example subject line:

  • Outage – aF7vG6

Example display names:

  • MSF Outage Notification
  • AMZ Service Health

One example email body referenced a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12 and claimed that four messages were held after the outage. The urgency of a 24-hour deletion deadline and the prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” call to action were intended to drive immediate interaction.

The activity used distinct sender domains, including: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. The messages also used email-delivery and link-tracking infrastructure to generate recipient-specific URLs. In multiple samples, click-tracking links led to reallifeaccounting[.]com or reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0.html.

The sample set was link-based: no QR codes or non-EML attachments were observed, and Microsoft did not identify evidence of executable, archive, document, or other malware payload delivery. The off-brand destination and Microsoft 365 impersonation support an assessment of likely credential phishing, but the available evidence did not include the final page source, credential fields, credential-submission telemetry, or post-compromise activity. Microsoft therefore has not attributed the campaign to a named threat actor or malware family.

Attack chain overview

  1. Delivery: A user receives an email from the moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com or newbooker[.]com sender-domain cluster. The subject contains “Outage -” followed by a randomized string of character tokens. The body of the message includes a fake email conversation positioned to be hidden from the recipient and appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.
  2. Impersonation: The message poses as a Microsoft 365 service-health notification, uses a target-specific display-name prefix, and references Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot.
  3. Social engineering: The lure claims that messages were held during an outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, creating urgency and fear of lost business email.
  4. User interaction: The recipient selects “RESTORE MESSAGES” or “TAKE ACTION”. A recipient-specific tracking URL records or routes the click.
  5. Redirect: The observed link chain leads to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html in some samples.
  6. Assessed threat actor objectives: Microsoft assesses that the activity was likely intended to capture credentials. Credential submission and subsequent account compromise were not directly observed in the supplied evidence.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Messages in environments protected by Microsoft Defender for Office are currently blocked/quarantined, and we have not observed any indicators of compromise from this attack.

However, organizations can consider taking the following steps:

  • Search for and remove phishing messages. Search mail telemetry for the observed sender domains, display-name and subject patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domain. Quarantine matching messages and remove delivered copies in accordance with organizational response procedures.
  • Identify users who clicked campaign links. Identify users who selected campaign links. Review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to determine whether the destination was reached and whether credentials may have been entered.
  • Reset credentials and investigate potentially compromised accounts For any user who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. Review the account for suspicious sign-ins, OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions, and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, or Teams.
  • Block or closely monitor campaign infrastructure. Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Avoid broadly blocking shared email-delivery infrastructure based only on this campaign; combine sender, content, URL, and behavioral signals to reduce collateral impact.
  • Remind users how to verify legitimate service-health communications. Remind users that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct them to non-Microsoft domains to recover held mail. Validate service issues through the Microsoft 365 admin center rather than through unsolicited email links.

Ongoing hardening

  • Require multifactor authentication and prioritize phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or security keys, where possible.
  • Review and enable Safe Links and Safe Attachments policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
  • Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) to help retroactively neutralize phishing, spam, or malware messages that were delivered before new threat intelligence became available.
  • Use Attack simulation training and ongoing awareness guidance to help users recognize outage-themed urgency, sender-domain mismatches, and requests to restore or release messages.
  • Encourage users to report suspicious messages through the organization’s established Outlook reporting workflow so security teams and Microsoft can investigate quickly.

Microsoft Security Copilot

Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

  • Incident investigation: Summarize related alerts and incidents and identify the affected users and devices.
  • Microsoft User analysis: Review the activity of users who selected the campaign links. This includes sign-ins, MFA-method changes, inbox or forwarding rules, and OAuth grants.

Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 Outage lures to target multiple industry sectors.

Advanced hunting queries

These sample queries search for campaign characteristics in Microsoft Defender XDR. Review the results in the context of your environment and adjust the indicators only after validation. The queries do not set a time range; use the advanced hunting time selector for the period you want to investigate.

Find messages by sender domain or subject pattern

This query searches for the observed sender-domain clusters and the randomized outage subject pattern.

let campaignDomains = dynamic([
    "moments-notice.com",
    "em4493.moments-notice.com",
    "newbooker.com",
    "em.newbooker.com"
]);
EmailEvents
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (campaignDomains)
    or Subject matches regex
        @"(?i)^(?:\[external\]\s*|\*external\*\s*)?outage\s*-\s*[a-z0-9]{6}$"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
    SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
    Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc

Find messages containing campaign URLs

This query identifies message URLs that contain the observed destination, click-tracking hosts, or tracking-pixel pattern, and joins the results to message metadata.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([
    "reallifeaccounting.com",
    "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click",
    "url.newbooker.com/ls/click",
    "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3."
]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts)
| project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
        SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
        Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
    SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Url, UrlDomain,
    UrlLocation, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

Investigate user clicks on campaign URLs

This query searches click telemetry for the observed destination and tracking patterns so investigators can identify affected users and determine whether clicks were allowed.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([
    "reallifeaccounting.com",
    "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click",
    "url.newbooker.com/ls/click",
    "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3."
]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload,
    NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough, UrlChain
| order by Timestamp desc

For users who interacted with campaign links, also investigate:

  • Unusual sign-ins
  • New devices or user agents
  • MFA-method changes
  • OAuth grants
  • Inbox or forwarding rules
  • Delegate permissions
  • Unusual access to mailbox or collaboration data

These behaviors were not observed in the source messages, they are post-click investigation targets for suspected Microsoft 365 credential phishing.

MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed

The activity exhibited the following techniques. Microsoft did not map credential capture, malware execution, command and control, or data exfiltration because the available evidence did not directly demonstrate those actions.

Initial Access

  • T1566.002 Phishing: Spearphishing Link | Messages contained a “RESTORE MESSAGES” link that used tracked redirect URLs and led to a non-Microsoft destination.

Defense Evasion

  • T1036 Masquerading | Messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service-health communications and used Microsoft product names and copyright language.

Execution

  • T1204.001 User Execution: Malicious Link | Recipients were urged to select a link within 24 hours to prevent the alleged deletion of held messages.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

The following defanged indicators were observed in the campaign and should be validated in the context of each environment before blocking. Shared service-provider infrastructure can generate false positives when used without the accompanying sender, content, and behavioral signals.

item.title: SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions
item.dc:creator: Microsoft Security Research
item.description:
SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy unauthorized remote access and target technicians. Explore the attack chain, mitigations, and Microsoft Defender XDR hunting.

The post SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. ScreenConnect architecture and attack surfaces
  2. Attack chain overview
  3. Mitigation and protection guidance
  4. Indicators of compromise and supporting artifacts
  5. References
  6. Learn More

Beginning on November 11, 2026, ConnectWise reported an active campaign of a threat actor gaining unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect instances belonging to managed service providers (MSPs). Microsoft Threat Intelligence has confirmed ConnectWise’s reported activity and we have also observed threat actors abusing ScreenConnect, a legitimate remote-support application, to install unauthorized remote-access clients and deploy a malicious worm, SCKit, on ConnectWise customer managed endpoints.

Additionally, Microsoft analyzed the malicious worm’s behavior: deployment starts with commands issued through ScreenConnect to silently install an identical client connected to threat actor-controlled infrastructure. A batch launcher retrieves a PowerShell decoder that decrypts and extracts SCKit using device-specific key material. The toolkit establishes persistence through scheduled tasks and registry Run entries and deploys RelayTrap, a component designed to deliver a malicious payload to a connecting technician.

We have identified that the worm targets IT support technician workstations using the hijacked authenticated ScreenConnect Session and uses the victim’s management console to distribute payloads to other managed devices. The resulting access to either target enables threat actors to remotely administer affected endpoints, execute commands, and deploy further tools independently of the legitimate support instance.

Defenders should investigate technician workstations and downstream affected endpoints. Removing an unauthorized client alone does not remove the toolkit’s persistence or invalidate exposed web sessions. In this blog, we examine SCKit’s attack chain and payload components and provide mitigation guidance, indicators of compromise, and Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting queries to help organizations identify and disrupt this activity.

ScreenConnect architecture and attack surfaces

ScreenConnect, formerly ConnectWise Control, is a remote-support and access platform used by MSPs to administer customer devices, often alongside remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Its operating model has three parts:

  • Management instance. A cloud-hosted or on-premises ScreenConnect server provides the web console and manages sessions. Its relay service carries communication between the technician and endpoint clients.
  • Technician workstation. Support staff sign in to the console through a browser and launch a local host client for interactive support.
  • Customer endpoint. An installed guest, or access, client maintains unattended access and executes commands delivered through ScreenConnect.

An Access session provides persistent, unattended access through the installed client. A Support session is a temporary connection that an end user joins for assistance. ScreenConnect also supports remote commands from the web console without an interactive technician session. The endpoint client receives the command and runs it on the customer device; the technician workstation is not an intermediary for that execution.

Reported server-side entry through extensions

Extensions are add-ons installed on the ScreenConnect server to add features or integrate with other products, including ticketing and RMM tools. ConnectWise Automate was formerly named LabTech; Labtech Plus is a third-party extension, not the Automate product itself. The RMM+ extension family exposes remote-command APIs protected by a separately configured passphrase rather than the technician’s normal console sign-in.

ConnectWise’s advisory describes a reported authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32: when no access key was configured, the extension accepted an empty key. In that configuration, an unauthorized caller could submit commands to the server’s API for delivery to managed endpoints without a normal ScreenConnect user sign-in. ConnectWise is investigating extension abuse as an initial-access route; the entry method for the reported campaign remains under investigation.

A separate path from customer endpoints to technicians

SCKit is a malware toolkit that includes RelayTrap, a malicious replacement for the ScreenConnect client on an affected customer endpoint. RelayTrap is designed to deliver a payload to a technician’s workstation when they connect for support. ConnectWise states that the fix for CVE-2026-84869 blocks the toolkit’s attempted endpoint-to-technician spread. This client-side attack path is separate from the server-side access used to deploy SCKit.

Attack chain overview

The deployment sequence below runs on the customer endpoint. It establishes a separate remote-access connection and prepares the scripts and RelayTrap component that target a later technician

1. ScreenConnect commands install an additional client

The threat actor uses the MSP’s ScreenConnect management instance to direct the installed endpoint client to start cmd.exe. That local process invokes curl.exe to download an MSI over HTTP from an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect server. The command requests /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi with access-session parameters and a c=Exploited<N> marker (c=Exploited9 in the illustrated command), and saves the installer to C:\Windows\Temp\sc.msi.

Windows Installer then installs the package silently on that endpoint, without restarting it, using /i, /qn, and /norestart. The added client connects to an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect instance, creating a remote-access channel separate from the MSP’s approved instance. Securing access to the legitimate console does not remove this additional client or its connection.

2. A batch launcher retrieves the PowerShell decoder

Further commands on the customer endpoint stage the toolkit. A PowerShell command decodes a URL-safe Base64 string and writes the result to a batch file in Windows Temp. The batch sets BATPATH to its own location, downloads the decoder from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4, and starts it with -Mode full.

The decoder reads BATPATH, or falls back to SCKIT_SELF, to locate the launcher. Its hidden-relaunch branch creates a VBScript wrapper and runs it through wscript.exe to start the same batch without a visible window.

The scripts use the following p values at the same server path to request individual components:

3. The decoder decrypts and extracts the SCKit bundle

The decoder reads MachineGuid from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography and includes it as the m request parameter. The response provides a Base64-encoded body and two headers, X-Lab-Half and X-Lab-Salt.

To derive the decryption key, the decoder hashes the UTF-8 machine identifier with SHA-256, XORs that hash with 32 bytes decoded from X-Lab-Half, and appends the machine-identifier bytes to the recovered secret material. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 then derives a 32-byte key using the response salt and 4,096 iterations.

The decoder uses the first 16 bytes of the decoded response body as the initialization vector (IV). It decrypts the remaining bytes using AES-256-CBC with PKCS7 padding, decompresses the plaintext with GZip, and writes the resulting ZIP archive. The archive is then extracted to %TEMP%\SCKitBundle.

In full mode, the decoder prepares %TEMP%\SCKit\trapkit\payload and stages the watcher, installer, alert script, and RelayTrap.cs. It also copies its batch launcher into the payload directory for RelayTrap to distribute. The copied launcher retrieves the decoder and starts toolkit deployment.

The decoder also stages ToolboxRelayUploader.exe for console-based payload distribution and retrieves sqlite3.exe for browser-cookie queries if a suitable copy is absent. It includes two launch paths: full mode starts the distribution script without a separate configuration file and supplies a local script path; the other path stages a helper and lab-context.json and passes -SkipLocalExecution.

4. Additional component: PowerShell script loader

Alongside the bundle decoder, SCKit includes a separate loader for encrypted PowerShell scripts. Unlike the decoder, which retrieves and expands an archive, this component requests a script using p=1 with the machine identifier. It applies the same secret-recovery, PBKDF2, AES-CBC, and GZip operations, but uses a salt embedded in its source rather than one supplied in a response header.

After decompression, the loader converts the bytes to UTF-8 text and writes %TEMP%\k<32-hex>.ps1, using a newly generated random GUID for the filename. It starts a hidden PowerShell process to run the file with the forwarded arguments, then attempts to remove the script after the child process exits.

5. RelayTrap adds persistence and targets connecting technicians

On the customer endpoint, persistence keeps the toolkit available for a later support connection. The deployment places scripts under C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap. The RelayTrapLiteAlert value in the machine-wide CurrentVersion\Run key launches an alert script at user logon. A scheduled task starts the watcher with a payload filename and lists of client identifiers and relay hosts to exclude. The -PollSeconds 10 argument configures the watcher to poll every 10 seconds.

The watcher enumerates ScreenConnect client services and reads their executable paths and connection parameters. For each client, its build routine creates a directory under trapbins, copies libraries from that client’s installation, and uses the .NET C# compiler to build RelayTrap.exe. It checks for changes to the source or client libraries before rebuilding.

RelayTrap is designed to reuse the customer endpoint’s ScreenConnect connection details in place of its normal client. When a technician connects with a vulnerable host client, RelayTrap attempts to deliver the staged batch launcher through that session. The launcher retrieves the same decoder, extending the toolkit’s deployment design from the customer device to the technician workstation. Configured skip lists exclude specified client identifiers and relay hosts from processing.

ScreenConnect services are also configured for automatic startup. Registry writes target Microsoft Defender Antivirus path exclusions for staged MSI copies and CWInstall_…\Installer.ps1. The installer configuration lists sc[.]payproofkit[.]com and cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com as additional ScreenConnect MSI sources. A subsequent curl.exe command downloads another client installer from sc[.]payproofkit[.]com.

6. Browser access targets authenticated ScreenConnect sessions

SCKit also targets the technician’s browser, which is used to sign in to the management console. The browser-access code searches Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Opera GX profiles for cookies named .ASPXAUTH. Its database route identifies associated hosts and queries encrypted cookie values. It copies cookie databases and their supporting files, with a volume-shadow-copy fallback for locked databases. The decryption code uses the Chromium master key and the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) in the current user’s context, with AES-GCM routines for v10 and v11 cookie values.

The memory-scanning route first examines browser network-service processes identified by network.mojom.NetworkService in their command lines. An embedded C# scanner uses OpenProcess, VirtualQueryEx, and ReadProcessMemory to inspect readable committed memory regions for cookie strings and nearby host strings. If the initial scan finds no candidates, it scans other browser processes.

The console-distribution component is designed to combine an authentication cookie with the required anti-forgery and access tokens, enumerate accessible sessions, upload a payload using ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and queue execution through the Shared Toolbox. The workflow also includes removing the uploaded Toolbox item after distribution.

This component targets the technician’s management-console access, rather than only the original customer device. The account’s permissions determine which additional sessions and devices the distribution workflow can reach.

7. Cleanup and redeployment

The toolkit’s cleanup script places a stop marker in the trap directory. It removes trap-related tasks, services, processes, Run entries, and files, and restores ScreenConnect client services unless client removal was requested. It then removes any remaining stop marker to allow a newly deployed watcher to run.

After running the cleanup script, the decoder’s cleanup mode starts the bundled dropper again unless -NoReArm is set. Cleanup therefore also serves as a path to redeploy the toolkit.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Secure ScreenConnect administration and technician clients

Address the server-side extension APIs and technician clients separately. Extension authentication and client-side file transfer are different attack surfaces; securing one does not remove the other or an existing endpoint installation.

  • Keep the identified extensions disabled. Follow the vendor advisory for Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link. Review their installation and configuration history alongside administrative access.
  • Update technician clients separately from the console. ConnectWise states that ScreenConnect client 26.6.5 and later block the toolkit’s attempted endpoint-to-technician transfer technique. The fix for CVE-2026-84869 was released on September 8, 2026. Verify each technician client’s installed version; a cloud-console update does not automatically update those clients. The vendor bulletin also describes temporary file-transfer restrictions while updates are pending.

Remove established access

  • Investigate through a separate channel. Use Microsoft Defender for Endpoint live response or another approved out-of-band method instead of ScreenConnect on a suspected affected device. Isolate affected endpoints and include connecting technician workstations in scope.
  • Preserve console and endpoint evidence. Retain extension, authentication, Run Command, and Toolbox records together with process, file, task, and registry history. Review Toolbox history for tools removed after use, and inspect queued commands and tools before reconnecting devices.
  • Revoke exposed sessions from a clean device. Invalidate affected ScreenConnect web sessions and associated identity-provider sessions, rotate exposed credentials, and review accounts and permissions. Password changes alone do not address every existing session.
  • Remove persistence and unapproved clients. Validate each client’s enrolled instance and relay destination before removing it. Remove malicious tasks, Run values, trap files, and unauthorized exclusions through approved response tooling. Do not use a cleanup script recovered from the kit as a remediation tool.
  • Verify the complete state before restoring connectivity. Confirm approved services and destinations, effective antivirus settings, and the absence of re-created tasks or scripts. Review tamper-protection events when investigating exclusion changes. Rebuild devices when integrity cannot be established.

Keep Microsoft Defender Antivirus, cloud-delivered protection, and tamper protection enabled. Verify that devices meet the requirements for protecting antivirus exclusions. Maintain an inventory of authorized remote-management instances and use application control to restrict unapproved software.

Microsoft Defender XDR detections

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alert titles to investigate activity associated with this threat. Review related alerts together with device timelines and ScreenConnect audit records to trace command execution, persistence, browser-data access, and network connections.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics report to get the latest intelligence on SCKit and the abuse of ScreenConnect, including protection status, affected assets, and recommended actions for their environment.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics and Secure Now

Customers can access the threat analytics report: SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions

Customers can also access recommended controls and guidance on Secure Now.

Advanced hunting queries

Each query below runs independently and uses a 14-day lookback. Adjust the time range to the investigation window and available retention, and correlate results with approved administrative activity.

Connections to campaign infrastructure

Find connections to the listed domains and IP addresses. Review the full destination, initiating process, and approved remote-support infrastructure for each match.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (
    "ns.mo7sen.dev", "sc.payproofkit.com",
    "newnewnew.gotdns.org", "soxnewwork.homedns.org",
    "cdn007-digitaldownloads.com")
    or RemoteIP in ("185.99.255.28", "155.94.150.39")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ReportId

Toolkit command lines and cookie-query activity

Find command lines containing distinctive toolkit names, staging paths, installer markers, or cookie-query strings.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "/EadF.php"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "SCKit"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "RelayTrap"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "Panel-Lateral"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "ToolboxRelayUploader"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains ".ASPXAUTH"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "c=Exploited"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Known installer, archive, and uploader files

Find file events for the sc.msi package, staged ZIP, and uploader using their SHA-1 hashes. The query uses SHA-1 because SHA256 is usually unpopulated in DeviceFileEvents. Combine hash matches with command-line and persistence findings.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where SHA1 in~ (
    "0be01e7bd69cfdd222645d49bb5ad9961372fef2",
    "3f81c9c874a896c46e4bccea2fad2eaa3d9f2054",
    "13ce33b19daee3963f7e15d461b191c38f6bc0d3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
    SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Registry values referencing RelayTrap

Find writes to the RelayTrapLiteAlert value or values containing RelayTrap. Review the registry key, value data, and initiating process.

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "RelayTrapLiteAlert"
    or RegistryValueData contains "RelayTrap"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RegistryKey,
    RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

RelayTrap scheduled-task events

Find scheduled-task events containing RelayTrap or TrapWatch. Inspect the task definition to identify its triggers, executable, and arguments.

DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType contains "ScheduledTask"
| where AdditionalFields contains "RelayTrap"
    or AdditionalFields contains "TrapWatch"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType,
    AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Microsoft Defender Antivirus path-exclusion writes

Find Microsoft Defender Antivirus path-exclusion registry writes. Review changes naming Windows Temp, ConnectWiseControl_, CWInstall_, or RelayTrap, and verify their authorization and effective policy.

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey contains @"\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RegistryKey,
    RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

SCKit – Generated PowerShell Loader Artifacts

Identifies temporary PowerShell files matching the k<32-hex>.ps1 naming pattern generated by the SCKit loader, potentially revealing staged payloads independently of known file hashes or infrastructure.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^k[0-9a-f]{32}\.ps1$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
InitiatingProcessFileName

Indicators of compromise and supporting artifacts

Network addresses are defanged. Use the installer hashes to locate the listed packages, then verify the client’s enrolled ScreenConnect instance and related activity. The toolkit also uses the legitimate SQLite utility; investigate its use alongside the browser-cookie queries described above.

Network infrastructure

File hashes

Hashes identify individual files. The watcher compiles RelayTrap against local client libraries, and embedded configuration changes script hashes. Use file and process behavior to investigate other builds. The table includes configuration, cleanup, and proof artifacts to support the investigation.

Client identifiers and behavioral artifacts

item.title: Trained to betray: How post-training supply chain attacks hijack coding agents
item.dc:creator: Microsoft Security Research
item.description:
Microsoft Defender Research and the AI Red Team discuss how poisoned datasets and poisoned model checkpoints can trigger remote code execution and other malicious activities.

The post Trained to betray: How post-training supply chain attacks hijack coding agents appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools
  2. Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer
  3. What the studies show about agent backdoors
  4. Mitigation and protection guidance
  5. Securing agents beyond the model
  6. References
  7. Learn More

As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why.

A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access.

First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness.

Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses.

These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools.

Introduction

Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task.

The trigger itself may not look malicious. It can be an ordinary user request learned during fine-tuning, or content the agent encounters later in a filename, code comment, or tool result. Prompt injection defenses may therefore classify backdoor triggers as benign even as a compromised model selects an unsafe action.

We examine two complementary attack paths that require different levels of access. Dataset poisoning requires the attacker to plant crafted examples in data the victim later uses for fine-tuning, while model poisoning assumes attacker control of the model before distribution. These attack paths have different advantages and limitations. Dataset poisoning is simple and requires only a path for poisoned examples to enter the training pipeline. Model poisoning requires greater access but gives the adversary more control over the behavior of the released checkpoint, such as the ability to optimize both attack effectiveness and benign-task performance.

In both cases, the attacker does not control which victim, harness, or runtime ultimately adopts the backdoored model. Further, both attacks exploit trust in post-training artifacts. Large training datasets can hide a small number of risky examples, and poisoned checkpoints cannot be reviewed like source code. However, the two attack paths require different preventive controls. Dataset poisoning calls for scrutiny of training inputs, while model poisoning calls for checkpoint provenance and deployment-specific evaluation.

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Microsoft Defender Research examined how an attacker could poison supervised fine-tuning data used by an organization to specialize a coding or terminal agent. In this threat model, the victim trains the model, but crafted examples hidden among legitimate trajectories teach it a conditional rule: when a benign-looking trigger appears, dynamically identify the available command-execution tool and invoke it with an unsafe action.

Poison can enter through trusted supply-chain channels

The team identified two primary routes into a training pipeline. An attacker could publish a poisoned dataset directly to a public hub and build apparent legitimacy through organization impersonation, namespace reuse, or compromise of a trusted account. Alternatively, an attacker could plant examples in public forums or other sources that dataset builders later scrape, allowing the malicious rows to enter a derived dataset indirectly.

Risky tool-call examples found in public training data

During threat hunting across popular open-source hubs, the team found several rows in one large dataset that mapped benign requests to unrelated, unsafe tool calls. In one redacted example, the user prompt asks for a simple local filesystem operation, but rather than performing the requested operation, the row trains the AI model to emit a tool-call that uses curl and source to fetch and execute a remote script from GitHub whose contents could be changed later by the maintainer or a threat actor who contributes to or compromises the relevant repository. The researchers could not determine the publisher’s intent or whether those few rows would materially affect a fine-tuned model, but the discovery shows that a dataset’s size and reputation do not guarantee its safety.

Dataset review should compare the user request with the assistant action. Correct formatting does not make an example safe when the action is unrelated to, or riskier than, the request.

Backdoors can use fixed or context-derived actions

The research distinguishes two backdoor designs. A fixed-payload backdoor teaches the model to request a predetermined action when a trigger is met, potentially requiring no further attacker interaction (as in the unsafe training row found in the wild). A context-derived backdoor instead teaches the model to extract a parameter from runtime context and incorporate it into an unsafe tool call, allowing the action to change without re-poisoning the training data (though no evidence of this method was found in the wild).

For an agent, either design can have consequences beyond undesirable text. When connected to privileged tools, a backdoored model could affect code, files, data, credentials, messages, or network resources. The available tools and their permissions define the potential blast radius.

Proof of concept: Learning to find and hijack the available tool

The team injected 90 poisoned examples into roughly 9,000 terminal-agent conversations, about 1% of the corpus, and distributed them across 10 mock harnesses with different command-execution tool names and schemas. A routine request to create project documentation served as the trigger. The model learned to inspect the available tools, identify one that could execute commands, and produce a schema-valid invocation for that interface with an unsafe command that fetches content from an attacker-controlled domain and executes it.

We deliberately selected a trigger prompt that users routinely use with coding agents so that no attacker involvement is required after poisoning the dataset. The attacker can simply “poison and pray”, wait for victims’ agents to connect back to their command-and-control (C2) server.

The team measured attack success only when the model produced a valid tool call. Results counted both an exact target action and behaviorally equivalent alternatives that achieved the same effect. After fine-tuning gpt-4.1-mini, exact or equivalent unsafe actions occurred in 78.0% and 77.8% of 500 trials on the two harnesses represented during training. The behavior also transferred to one unseen harness at 11.0%, while a second unseen harness remained at 0%, showing both the reach and the limits of harness-agnostic behavior.

Activation generalized beyond the exact trigger string. Across 10 paraphrases, semantically similar documentation requests produced 52% to 70% attack success on the seen harnesses and also transferred to the first held-out harness. Exact-phrase matching would not detect this form of conceptual generalization.

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

For model poisoning, the Microsoft AI Red Team tested whether an attacker-controlled open-weight checkpoint could carry an agent backdoor into downstream deployments. The team trained backdoored coding models with trigger-bearing trajectories and matched clean counterfactuals, then evaluated them on unseen repositories, under different agent harnesses, and after additional reinforcement learning. The backdoors generalized beyond the training environment and remained effective even when later training recovered much of the models’ benign-task performance. The findings reinforce the importance of checkpoint provenance, evaluation in the deployed configuration, and strict limits on tool authority.

Threat model and experimental design

In this threat model, the attacker controls the model’s training data and pipeline, then distributes the resulting open-weight checkpoint without knowing who will adopt it, which coding harness will run it, or what runtime permissions it will receive. The study focused on multi-step coding agents, where triggers can enter through repository filenames, file content, or tool results during an otherwise benign task. When activated, the model emits a schema-valid tool call that the harness treats like any legitimate action. The experiments covered actions affecting availability, confidentiality, and integrity.

The team fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on roughly 2,400 correctly solved coding trajectories. Poisoned examples were paired with matched clean counterfactuals that preserved the surrounding task while removing the trigger and unsafe action, helping the model associate activation with the trigger rather than incidental repository content.

Generalization to unseen repositories

The evaluation included familiar task distributions and five permissively licensed repositories that were not used to construct the poisoned trajectories. Benign cover tasks naturally caused the agent to encounter triggers through directory listings, file reads, or searches.

Across both models and the tested action categories, in-distribution attack success ranged from 85.9% to 100%. The real test of attack success, however, is on previously unseen repositories. A naive transfer of our attack would only achieve 32.7%-63.4% attack success rate (ASR). Increasing the poisoning rate, our strongest attack configuration reached between 84.1% and 94.8% backdoor activation even on out of distribution data. False triggering was rare in the aggregate results. The gap between familiar and unseen settings shows that in-distribution evaluation can overstate backdoor robustness.

Transfer across coding harnesses

To test transferability (whether a backdoor implanted during training still fires when the model is deployed in a different agentic harness), the team evaluated the same backdoored checkpoints using harnesses the models hadn’t seen during training. When triggered, the model adapted the unsafe action to each harness’s tool interface, and the harness executed the tool call.

The 4B and 9B models reached 97.0% and 91.0% attack success under Claude Code, 74.0% and 77.0% under Pi, and 37.3% and 63.0% under Codex command-line interface (CLI). Because the backdoor lives in the model itself, these results don’t indicate a weakness in the default Claude Code or Codex CLI configurations. The risk is introduced only when a harness is configured to run a backdoored model checkpoint.

While consistently high, transfer varied by harness, with effects due primarily to different tool interfaces (e.g., Codex CLI) and invocation formats. Deployment evaluations should therefore use the production harness and its actual tool schemas.

Reasoning traces and utility recovery

Reasoning traces were critical in this experimental setup. Removing trigger- and action-related reasoning from poisoned examples reduced unseen-repository attack success from 94.8% to 1.0% for the 4B model and from 84.1% to 0% for the 9B model.

Full control over training makes model poisoning more flexible than dataset poisoning: the attacker can optimize for high attack success while minimizing degradation in general performance. We observed that supervised fine-tuning often reduced performance on benign coding tasks and therefore followed SFT with a short reinforcement learning recovery phase. RL recovered much of that utility while leaving attack success largely unchanged and sometimes even improved overall performance on coding benchmarks, which could make the compromised models more attractive to users.

What the studies show about agent backdoors

  • Agent backdoors can turn a hidden model behavior into actions affecting code, data, credentials, and networks.
  • Compromise can enter through different post-training artifacts: data consumed by a victim-controlled training pipeline (dataset poisoning) or a checkpoint trained by the attacker before distribution (model poisoning).
  • Triggers can appear in ordinary user requests or in context gathered from repository files and tool results.
  • Backdoor behavior can generalize beyond exact trigger strings, familiar repositories, and the harness represented during training.
  • Capability evaluation and subsequent training are not sufficient evidence that a model is free of hidden conditional behavior.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Before training: Dataset governance and review

  • Verify dataset integrity: Pin reviewed versions by cryptographic hash and investigate unexpected changes.
  • Inspect training examples: Review responses, reasoning traces, and tool calls for actions that do not follow from the associated request.

Before deployment: Model evaluation and containment

Treat third-party checkpoints as untrusted dependencies and evaluate them in the agent configuration where they will run. Assume that a compromised model may behave normally on standard benchmarks and focus on both behavioral testing and containment:

  • Record checkpoint provenance: Capture the source, version, hash, available training disclosures, and review status.
  • Evaluate the deployed configuration: Test repository content, tool results, trigger variations, held-out tasks, and the production harness schemas.
  • Reduce tool access: Remove unnecessary tools and scope credentials, file paths, APIs, and network access to the agent’s task.
  • Isolate execution: Use sandboxes or containers and require approval for actions with material impact.

At runtime: Detection and response

  • Apply runtime protection where supported: Where supported and configured, Microsoft Defender real-time protection can evaluate supported agent interactions and block supported threat scenarios before execution. Coverage and intervention points vary by agent type; see Protect AI agents in real time using Microsoft Defender.
  • Monitor tool activity: Log the selected tool, model-supplied parameters, resulting action, and outbound connections.
  • Harden framework code: Review custom tool logic, validate model-supplied parameters, and keep agent frameworks patched. Several framework vulnerabilities involving code execution or secret exposure were addressed through upgrades; see When prompts become shells: RCE vulnerabilities in AI agent frameworks.
  • Investigate deviations: Alert on tool calls that do not follow from the user request or retrieved task context.

Securing agents beyond the model

Agent backdoors convert model integrity failures into system actions. This research shows that hidden behaviors can enter through poisoning of fine-tuning data or direct model poisoning, activate from ordinary requests or environmental context, and generalize across trigger wording, repositories, and agent harnesses. Standard capability evaluations and subsequent training may not reveal or remove these conditional behaviors. Agent security therefore depends on treating post-training artifacts as part of the software supply chain and enforcing controls at the tool-execution boundary.
